summary: 9b continues the aggadic examination of Temple destruction. The bizayon kodashim (desecration of offerings) by Eli's sons is detailed, completing the Shiloh account from 9a. The First Temple's three cardinal sins are then proven from separate verses. The Second Temple's sinat chinam (baseless hatred) is declared equivalent to all three, while the corrupt First Temple generation is described as relying on God and receiving three decrees corresponding to its three sins. A challenge that the First Temple also had sinat chinam is answered by restricting it to the nesi'im (leaders). R. Yochanan and R. Elazar state that revealed sin had a revealed end to exile, while unrevealed sin did not. Reish Lakish argues that the later generations were greater because they studied Torah under foreign rule, but R. Yochanan answers that the rebuilt Temple proves the earlier generation's superiority, and R. Elazar gives the same answer. Finally, Reish Lakish rebukes Babylonian Jewry for not returning en masse with Ezra. The wall/door and silver/cedar imagery, sasmagor, and the bat kol are explained; the reported participants are corrected; and R. Yochanan rejects Reish Lakish's explanation, saying that even a complete return would not have caused the Shechina to rest in the Second Temple. His proof begins but is cut off at the end of the daf and continues on 10a.

display.title: Eli's sons: delayed bird-offerings and desecration of sacrifices
display.oneLine: The two sins of Eli's sons are detailed: delaying women's bird-offerings (treated by scripture as sexual immorality) and taking raw meat before the fat was burned (degradation of sacred offerings).
display.shortSummary: Eli's sons' delay of women's bird-offerings: although they did not commit adultery, their delay kept women at the Tabernacle and thus separated from their husbands - scripture holds them accountable as if they had cohabited with the women. Their second sin: bizayon kodashim. Before the fat of an offering was burned on the altar, a servant of the priests would come and demand raw meat for roasting. The man bringing the sacrifice would protest: 'Let them first burn the fat today, then take whatever you wish.' The servant would say: 'No, give it now or I will take it by force.' This brazen taking of raw, unburned meat was the desecration.
display.whats: This section closes the account of Shiloh's sins. The delay of bird-offerings kept women waiting and away from their husbands; the raw-meat taking showed contempt for the sacrificial order and threatened worshippers with force.
display.hint: The raw-meat verse says they took it 'before the fat was burned' - why does that specific sequencing make the taking a desecration rather than just a rude request?

learning.learnerQuestion: Why does scripture treat the delay of bird-offerings as equivalent to adultery?
learning.coreTension: Eli's sons did not literally cohabit with the women, yet scripture treats the delay of their offerings as though they had. The delay kept the women at Shiloh and away from their husbands.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara distinguishes the literal act from scriptural attribution in this case: because Eli's sons delayed the bird-offerings and thereby delayed the women from returning home, scripture treats them as though they had cohabited with the women.
learning.resolution: The two sins of Shiloh are established: delayed bird-offerings, treated by scripture as though Eli's sons had cohabited with the women, and taking raw meat prematurely, identified as bizayon kodashim.

takeaway.text: Eli's sons did not literally cohabit with the women, but their delay kept the women from returning to their husbands, so scripture treats this delay as though they had.

reasoningPattern.notes: The Gemara explains why scripture uses the language of cohabitation here even though the underlying act was delaying the women's offerings.

learning.ahaMoment: The raw-meat scene is vivid: a worshipper brings an animal, the priest's servant demands raw meat, the worshipper protests, the servant says 'give it now or I take it by force.' This is Temple service turned extortion - a shocking portrait of institutional corruption.
learning.learningBlocker: The passage establishes that Eli's sons delayed the bird-offerings and thereby kept the women waiting. It does not specify how long the delay lasted or describe the precise processing mechanics.
learning.memoryAnchor: Two Eli-sons sins: delay the kanim (bird-offerings) - women stuck waiting and kept from their husbands, so scripture treats the delay as cohabitation. Take raw meat before the fat is burned - intimidation and desecration of the offerings.

argumentFlow.label: Delayed bird-offerings kept women impure; scripture attributes the sin
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: Eli's sons delayed the processing of women's bird-offerings. Since the women had to wait, they could not achieve purity and could not return to their husbands. Scripture treats the priests as if they had committed the act of cohabitation themselves.

sourceRefs.note: Delayed bird-offerings attributed as giluy arayot

argumentFlow.label: Bizayon kodashim: raw meat seized before fat was burned
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The desecration: a servant of the priests would demand raw meat before the fat was burned on the altar. The worshipper would protest. The servant would say: 'Give it now or I will take it by force.' This brazen seizing of raw meat - before the proper sacrificial sequence - was the bizayon kodashim.

sourceRefs.note: Bizayon kodashim scene detailed

visualizableElements.item: A worshipper bringing an animal to the altar; a priest's servant aggressively demanding raw, uncooked meat before the fat is burned; the worshipper protesting; the servant threatening force. Captures the extortion aspect of bizayon kodashim.
visualizableElements.label: Raw meat seizure scene

quizSeeds.question: Why does scripture treat the delay of women's bird-offerings as equivalent to sexual immorality?
quizSeeds.answer: Because delaying the offerings kept the women at the Tabernacle and away from their husbands. Scripture therefore treats Eli's sons as though they had cohabited with the women, even though they did not literally do so.

quizSeeds.question: What was the specific act of bizayon kodashim by Eli's sons?
quizSeeds.answer: Their servants would demand raw meat before the fat of the offering was burned on the altar. If the worshipper refused, they would take the meat by force. This violated the sacrificial order and treated sacred meat as personal property.

misconceptions.misconception: Eli's sons refused to accept women's bird-offerings entirely.
misconceptions.correction: The Gemara says they delayed the offerings, causing the women to wait and delaying their return to their husbands. It does not specify a refusal, a precise duration, or detailed processing mechanics.

prerequisiteKnowledge: The distinction between literal and attributed sin in Talmudic reading

display.title: First Temple: three cardinal sins, each independently proven
display.oneLine: The First Temple was destroyed for avodah zarah, giluy arayot, and shefichut damim (three cardinal sins) - each independently proven from its own verse.
display.shortSummary: The Gemara states that the First Temple was destroyed for three things: avodah zarah (idolatry), giluy arayot (sexual immorality), and shefichut damim (bloodshed). Each is supported by a biblical verse. Idolatry: 'the bed is too short for both to lie' (Isaiah) - R. Yonatan reads this as the Sanctuary becoming too narrow once an idol shared the space with God; R. Shmuel bar Nachmani says R. Yonatan wept when he reached this teaching. Sexual immorality: the Gemara expounds Isaiah's daughters-of-Zion verse phrase by phrase, with R. Yitzchak interpreting its final phrase as hiding myrrh and balsam in their shoes and kicking the scent toward young men. Bloodshed: the cited verse says Manasseh shed very much innocent blood; the sentence continues into the next sugya.
display.whats: The Gemara grounds the First Temple's three-sin charge in separate biblical passages: the narrow-bed exposition for idolatry, Isaiah's daughters of Zion for sexual immorality, and Manasseh's innocent blood for bloodshed.
display.hint: The passage charges the First Temple generation with three grave sins at once - how does the Gemara prove each one from the text?

learning.learnerQuestion: The passage charges the First Temple generation with idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed - what specific verse proves each of these three sins?
learning.coreTension: A blanket charge of three grave sins needs textual support. How does the Gemara derive idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed from Scripture, and how is each phrase of the daughters-of-Zion verse used in the sexual-immorality proof?
learning.coreMove: For idolatry, R. Yonatan reads 'the bed is too short for both to stretch out' (Isaiah) as describing the Sanctuary itself: a space built for one that became too narrow once an idol shared it with God - R. Shmuel bar Nachmani reports that R. Yonatan wept upon reaching this teaching. For sexual immorality, the Gemara expounds Isaiah's description of the daughters of Zion phrase by phrase, with R. Yitzchak interpreting the final phrase as hiding myrrh and balsam in their shoes and kicking the scent toward young men. For bloodshed, the cited verse states that Manasseh shed very much innocent blood.
learning.resolution: The three-sin charge is grounded: idolatry from the narrow-bed verse, sexual immorality from the daughters-of-Zion catalogue including R. Yitzchak's exposition of its final phrase, and bloodshed from the verse stating that Manasseh shed very much innocent blood. The verse's sentence continues into the next sugya.

takeaway.text: The charge that the First Temple fell for idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed is supported by separate passages: the narrow bed for idolatry, the daughters of Zion for immorality, and the verse stating that Manasseh shed very much innocent blood for bloodshed.

reasoningPattern.notes: The passage matches each named sin to its own independent proof-text rather than relying on one verse for the three-part charge.

learning.ahaMoment: Each sin is matched to scriptural evidence: the narrow bed depicts the Sanctuary sharing space with a rival, Isaiah's daughters-of-Zion catalogue is expounded phrase by phrase, and Manasseh's verse says he shed very much innocent blood.
learning.learningBlocker: R. Yitzchak is interpreting the final phrase of the daughters-of-Zion verse, 'with their feet they would tinkle.' His perfume account belongs to the phrase-by-phrase exposition itself.
learning.memoryAnchor: Three sins, three proofs: a bed too narrow for two (idolatry), the daughters of Zion's provocative walk (immorality), and Manasseh shedding very much innocent blood (bloodshed).

quizSeeds.answer: Avodah zarah (idolatry), giluy arayot (sexual immorality), and shefichut damim (bloodshed).

display.title: Second Temple destroyed for sinat chinam; First Temple generation trusted in God despite its sins
display.oneLine: The Second Temple generation studied Torah and practiced kindness, yet was destroyed for sinat chinam - declared equal to all three cardinal sins combined; the passage then notes that the First Temple generation, wicked as it was, still trusted in God, and traces the three decrees God brought upon them to their three sins.
display.shortSummary: The Second Temple generation engaged in Torah study, mitzvot, and acts of kindness. Why was the Temple destroyed? For sinat chinam (baseless hatred). This teaches that sinat chinam equals the three cardinal sins combined. The Gemara then returns to the First Temple generation: wicked as they were, they still trusted in God - proven by Micah 3:11, where even corrupt heads, priests, and prophets say 'is the Lord not among us? No evil shall befall us.' Therefore God brought upon them three decrees corresponding to their three sins, per Micah 3:12: Zion plowed as a field, Jerusalem in heaps, and the Temple Mount like the high places of a forest.
display.whats: The passage states that sinat chinam is weighed against the three cardinal sins together, without explaining the measure of that equivalence. It then returns to the First Temple generation: despite its wickedness it relied on God, and God brought three decrees corresponding to its three sins.
display.hint: How can a generation of Torah scholars and practitioners of kindness be destroyed for the same reason as a generation charged with idolatry, sexual immorality, and bloodshed?

learning.learnerQuestion: How can sinat chinam be equal to all three cardinal sins combined, and what does the passage then say about the First Temple generation's own trust in God?
learning.coreTension: The Second Temple generation practiced Torah, mitzvot, and kindness, yet its Temple was destroyed for sinat chinam. The Gemara weighs that hatred against all three sins named for the First Temple, then turns back to the earlier generation's surprising reliance on God despite its corruption.
learning.coreMove: The Gemara states the equivalence without supplying a causal theory for it. It then cites Micah 3:11 to show corrupt leaders still saying that God was among them, followed by Micah 3:12 and three decrees corresponding to the three sins in their hands.
learning.resolution: Sinat chinam is stated to equal the three cardinal sins together. The First Temple generation's three sins are then matched to three decrees - Zion as a field, Jerusalem as heaps, and the Temple Mount as forest high places. The next sugya asks whether the First Temple was truly free of sinat chinam.

takeaway.text: Torah, mitzvot, and kindness did not prevent destruction when sinat chinam was present; the Gemara weighs that hatred against the First Temple's three sins together. It then matches those three earlier sins with three decrees.

reasoningPattern.notes: The Gemara states that sinat chinam is weighed against the three cardinal sins together but does not explain the metric of comparison.

learning.ahaMoment: A generation explicitly described as studying Torah, observing mitzvot, and practicing kindness still loses the Temple because of sinat chinam, which the Gemara weighs against the three First Temple sins together.
learning.learningBlocker: Students may think the Second Temple generation was hypocritical - that they did not really practice Torah and mitzvot. The Talmud affirms they genuinely did; their failure was internal (hatred of each other), not external.
learning.memoryAnchor: Second Temple: Torah + mitzvot + kindness, yet destroyed for sinat chinam, weighed against all three cardinal sins. First Temple: wicked, yet still relied on God (Micah 3:11); three decrees correspond to its three sins (Micah 3:12).

quizSeeds.question: How does the Talmud explain that the Second Temple generation - who studied Torah and performed kindness - was destroyed?
quizSeeds.answer: Because of sinat chinam (baseless hatred), which the Gemara says is weighed against all three cardinal sins combined. The passage does not supply a separate theory for how that equivalence is measured.

quizSeeds.question: What does Micah 3:11 prove about the First Temple generation, and what does Micah 3:12 explain?
quizSeeds.answer: Micah 3:11 shows that even the corrupt leadership relied on God ('is the Lord not among us?'). Micah 3:12 supplies the three decrees - field, ruins, and forest high places - corresponding to their three sins.

misconceptions.misconception: The Second Temple generation was hypocritical - they did not really practice Torah and mitzvot.
misconceptions.correction: The Talmud affirms they genuinely studied Torah, performed mitzvot, and practiced kindness. Their failure was not external behavior but internal: hatred of each other.

misconceptions.misconception: Sinat chinam is worse than murder or idolatry in terms of individual severity.
misconceptions.correction: The passage says sinat chinam is weighed against the three sins together, but it does not define that equivalence as either individual severity or communal destructive capacity.

display.title: First Temple sinat chinam: confined to the nesi'im
display.oneLine: A challenge - wasn't there sinat chinam in the First Temple too? - is answered: R. Eliezer identifies it as leaders who ate and drank together while slandering each other, and a baraita confirms it was confined to the nesi'im (leaders), not the general population.
display.shortSummary: But wait - was the First Temple free of sinat chinam entirely? A verse (Ezekiel: 'terrors of the sword are among my people; therefore strike your thigh') suggests otherwise. R. Eliezer explains: these are people who eat and drink with each other, yet stab each other with the swords of their tongues (slander). A baraita then confirms via the verse 'cry and wail, son of man, for it was against My people' that this applied specifically to the nesi'im (leaders and princes) of Israel, not the population generally.
display.whats: This section qualifies the sinat chinam argument: it was not entirely absent from the First Temple era. R. Eliezer describes people eating and drinking together while attacking one another with words, and the baraita restricts the cited behavior to Israel's princes.
display.hint: How does the baraita narrow the apparent evidence that sinat chinam also existed in the First Temple era?

learning.learnerQuestion: How does the Gemara answer the evidence that sinat chinam also existed in the First Temple era?
learning.coreTension: The sinat chinam argument seems to break down: both Temple eras had sinat chinam. The Gemara resolves this with a scope question: who exactly harbored the hatred?
learning.coreMove: R. Eliezer identifies the First Temple's sinat chinam concretely: people who ate and drank together while stabbing each other with slanderous words. A baraita then narrows the verse's target: it applied specifically to the nesi'im (leaders), not the general population.
learning.resolution: The First Temple's sinat chinam is confirmed but scoped: confined to the leadership. Whether and how this changes the exile-length picture is developed in the next sugya.

takeaway.text: A sweeping claim (sinat chinam destroyed only the Second Temple) survives a direct challenge by being scoped rather than abandoned: the First Temple did have sinat chinam, but confined to its leadership.

reasoningPattern.notes: The Gemara answers the broad challenge by restricting the verse's target to the princes of Israel.

learning.ahaMoment: R. Eliezer's image is vivid: people literally eating and drinking together while 'stabbing' each other with slander - sinat chinam does not require open conflict, only two-faced sociability.
learning.learningBlocker: The passage establishes a scope distinction - the cited hatred was among the princes - but does not itself explain the later exile endpoint through that social scope.
learning.memoryAnchor: First Temple sinat chinam: real, but R. Eliezer locates it as leaders eating/drinking together while slandering each other, and a baraita confirms it was confined to the nesi'im, not the general population.

display.title: Revealed sin gets a revealed end; R. Yochanan and Reish Lakish dispute generational merit
display.oneLine: R. Yochanan and R. Elazar together teach that a generation whose sin is revealed gets a revealed end to its exile, while a generation whose sin is hidden does not; R. Yochanan then prefers the earlier generation, Reish Lakish argues for the later one, and R. Yochanan answers with the rebuilt Temple as proof.
display.shortSummary: Completing the baraita: the verse 'cry and wail, son of man' was specifically about the nesi'im of Israel. R. Yochanan and R. Elazar both taught: the earlier generations, whose sin was revealed, had their end [of exile] revealed; the later generations, whose sin was not revealed, did not have their end revealed. R. Yochanan then preferred the earlier generations. Reish Lakish objected that the later generations were greater because they studied Torah under foreign rule. R. Yochanan answered that the restored Temple proves the earlier generation's superiority. Students then asked R. Elazar which generation was greater; his answer begins 'set your eyes...' at the end of this range and completes with the Temple building at the start of the next sugya.
display.whats: R. Yochanan and R. Elazar correlate revealed sin with a revealed end to exile and concealed sin with an undisclosed end. R. Yochanan answers Reish Lakish's generational-merit argument with the restored Temple. R. Elazar is asked the same question, but the referent of his answer appears just beyond this sugya's boundary.
display.hint: Why would a generation whose sin was openly visible get a clearer end to its punishment than a generation whose sin stayed hidden?

learning.learnerQuestion: Why does a generation whose sin was revealed get a revealed end to its exile, while a generation whose sin was hidden does not?
learning.coreTension: The earlier generation's sin was exposed and its exile endpoint was disclosed, while the later generation's sin was concealed and its endpoint remained undisclosed. The Gemara states this correlation without explaining a repentance or rebuke mechanism.
learning.coreMove: R. Yochanan and R. Elazar state the principle jointly. R. Yochanan then makes his own value judgment (earlier generations are preferable), which Reish Lakish directly challenges (later generations achieve more, given their harder circumstances). R. Yochanan's rebuttal appeals to an external, verifiable fact: the Temple was rebuilt for the earlier generation, not for the later one.
learning.resolution: The revealed-sin/revealed-end correlation is established. Reish Lakish argues that the later generations are greater because they study Torah under foreign rule, and R. Yochanan answers with the restored Temple. R. Elazar's response begins at this sugya's final line but names its witness only in the next sugya.

takeaway.text: The earlier generation's exposed sin corresponded to a disclosed exile endpoint; the later generation's concealed sin corresponded to an undisclosed endpoint. The passage states the correlation without supplying its mechanism.

reasoningPattern.notes: The structural principle pairs exposed sin with a disclosed end and concealed sin with an undisclosed end, without adding a causal mechanism.

learning.ahaMoment: Reish Lakish points to Torah study under foreign rule as evidence for the later generations, while R. Yochanan answers with the earlier generation's restored Temple. The page division splits R. Elazar's answer between this sugya and the next.
learning.learningBlocker: R. Yochanan's Temple-building answer is complete here. R. Elazar's separate answer is not: line 39 says only 'set your eyes,' and line 40 supplies 'on the Temple building.'
learning.memoryAnchor: Revealed sin -> revealed end; hidden sin -> no revealed end. R. Yochanan: earlier generations greater, proven by the restored Temple. Reish Lakish: later generations greater because they study Torah under oppression. R. Elazar's answer starts here and completes in the next sugya.

visualizableElements.item: Reish Lakish argues for the later generations from Torah study under oppression; R. Yochanan answers from the restored Temple; R. Elazar's separate answer begins here and crosses into the next sugya.
visualizableElements.label: Generational-merit dispute

quizSeeds.question: What principle do R. Yochanan and R. Elazar state together about revealed vs. hidden sin?
quizSeeds.answer: A generation whose sin was revealed gets a revealed end to its exile (the First Temple's 70 years); a generation whose sin was hidden does not get a revealed end (the Second Temple's sinat chinam).

quizSeeds.question: What is R. Yochanan's proof that the earlier generations were greater, and how far does R. Elazar's answer proceed within this sugya?
quizSeeds.answer: R. Yochanan points to the Temple building: it was restored to the earlier generation but not to the later one. R. Elazar's answer begins 'set your eyes...' here, but the Temple building is named only at the start of the next sugya.

misconceptions.misconception: R. Elazar's complete Temple-building answer appears within this sugya's lines 35-39.
misconceptions.correction: Only 'set your eyes...' appears by line 39. The words identifying the Temple building as the witness occur on line 40, at the start of the next sugya.

display.title: Reish Lakish rebukes Babylonian Jewry in the Jordan; sasmagor and bat kol explained
display.oneLine: Reish Lakish, swimming in the Jordan, denounces Babylonian Jewry for not returning en masse with Ezra, applying Song of Songs' wall/door and silver/cedar imagery; sasmagor and the bat kol are explained; the Gemara questions and resolves who was actually in the river, then cuts off mid-thought on a further point about Ezra's generation, continuing on 10a.
display.shortSummary: R. Elazar's answer completes: 'your witness is the Temple building.' Reish Lakish was swimming in the Jordan River; Rabbah bar bar Chana extended a hand to him, and Reish Lakish rebuked Babylonian Jewry through Song of Songs' wall/door and silver/cedar imagery for not returning together with Ezra. Ulla explains sasmagor as cedar rot, and R. Abba connects it to the bat kol that remained after prophecy departed. The Gemara questions the reported participants; Rav Papa proposes either Reish Lakish with Ze'iri or R. Elazar with Rabbah bar bar Chana. When Reish Lakish reported his teaching to R. Yochanan, R. Yochanan rejected its causal explanation: even had everyone returned with Ezra, the Shechina would not have rested in the Second Temple. His proof from 'may God enlarge Yefet, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem' begins but is cut off at the end of 9b.
display.whats: This closing passage presents Reish Lakish's incomplete-return explanation through the cedar/sasmagor and bat kol imagery, then records R. Yochanan's rejection of that explanation: even a complete return would not have brought the Shechina to the Second Temple. The proof for R. Yochanan's position begins but is cut off at the daf boundary.
display.hint: By the time 9b ends, has the Gemara finished explaining its final point about Ezra's generation and the Shechina - or has it only just introduced it?

learning.learnerQuestion: Why is Reish Lakish so harsh toward Babylonian Jewry, and how far does the daf's final point about Ezra's generation actually get explained?
learning.coreTension: Reish Lakish attributes the diminished result to Babylonian Jewry's incomplete return with Ezra, using the wall/door and silver/cedar imagery. R. Yochanan rejects that causal account and says the Shechina would not have rested in the Second Temple even after a complete return.
learning.coreMove: Wall = unified complete return = silver (imperishable). Door = partial return = cedar (some solid, some rot). Ulla and R. Abba specify what that rot is: a literal worm (sasmagor), and allegorically the bat kol that replaced full prophecy. A critical aside then questions the story's own transmission (would Reish Lakish really speak with Rabbah bar bar Chana?), resolved by Rav Papa proposing alternate pairings - with the swimmer and hand-extender specifically swapped in the second option, not merely relabeled.
learning.resolution: The participant question receives Rav Papa's alternate pairings. R. Yochanan then rejects Reish Lakish's causal explanation and states that even a complete return would not have brought the Shechina to the Second Temple. His scriptural proof begins but is not completed on 9b.

takeaway.text: Historical rebuke in the Talmud can rest on precise, dual-layered imagery (a literal worm and an allegorical diminishment of prophecy) while the underlying story's own transmission is treated with critical scrutiny, not taken at face value.

reasoningPattern.notes: The same daf-boundary pattern seen elsewhere in this campaign: a final point is introduced but not completed, continuing to the next daf.

learning.ahaMoment: The Gemara does not just tell the Jordan story - it interrupts itself to ask whether the story's own cast of characters is even correct, given what is independently known about Reish Lakish's selectiveness in his associations. Rav Papa's resolution swaps BOTH who swam and who extended the hand between the two proposed pairings, not just the names.
learning.learningBlocker: R. Yochanan's 'that is not the reason' rejects Reish Lakish's explanation about the incomplete return; it is not a dismissal of the participant question. His contrary claim is stated on 9b, while its proof continues on 10a.
learning.memoryAnchor: Reish Lakish: wall+silver = complete return; door+cedar = partial return, with sasmagor and bat kol. Rav Papa supplies two possible participant pairings. R. Yochanan rejects the incomplete-return explanation: even a complete return would not have brought the Shechina to the Second Temple; his proof continues on 10a.

argumentFlow.label: Reish Lakish in the Jordan denounces Babylonian Jewry
argumentFlow.speaker: Reish Lakish
argumentFlow.text: R. Elazar's answer completes: 'your witness is the Temple building.' Reish Lakish was swimming in the Jordan River. Rabbah bar bar Chana came and extended a hand to him. Reish Lakish said: 'I despise you [Babylonians]!' - quoting Song of Songs 8:9: if she is a wall, we will build upon her a turret of silver; if she is a door, we will enclose her with a cedar board.

sourceRefs.note: R. Elazar's answer completes; Reish Lakish's Jordan River rebuke begins

argumentFlow.label: Wall vs. door explained: silver vs. cedar
argumentFlow.speaker: Reish Lakish
argumentFlow.text: Applied: had all Babylonian Jews ascended together with Ezra (like a wall - unified), they would have been likened to silver, which rot cannot touch. Since they ascended only partially (like a door), they are likened to cedar, which rot can reach.

sourceRefs.note: Wall/door metaphor applied: silver vs. cedar

argumentFlow.label: Sasmagor: Ulla explains the rot, R. Abba identifies it with the bat kol
argumentFlow.speaker: Ulla / R. Abba
argumentFlow.text: What is the 'cedar'-rot? Ulla said: sasmagor, a worm that hollows cedar from within. What is sasmagor? R. Abba said: it alludes to the bat kol - once the last prophets (Chagai, Zechariah, Malachi) died, the Ruach HaKodesh departed from Israel, but they still made use of the bat kol.

sourceRefs.note: Sasmagor explained by Ulla, identified with bat kol by R. Abba

argumentFlow.label: Gemara questions the story: would Reish Lakish really speak with Rabbah bar bar Chana?
argumentFlow.speaker: Gemara
argumentFlow.text: The Gemara objects: Reish Lakish was famously selective about his associates - he would not even converse with R. Elazar, the master of the Land of Israel. Whoever he DID converse with was trusted implicitly for business loans without witnesses. Would he really have conversed with Rabbah bar bar Chana?

sourceRefs.note: Critical question about the story's transmission

argumentFlow.label: Rav Papa: a third party - two alternate pairings, swimmer and hand-extender both swapped
argumentFlow.speaker: Rav Papa
argumentFlow.text: Rav Papa resolved the participant question: either Reish Lakish was swimming and Ze'iri extended the hand, or R. Elazar was swimming and Rabbah bar bar Chana extended the hand. Reish Lakish later reported his teaching to R. Yochanan, who rejected Reish Lakish's causal explanation.

sourceRefs.note: Rav Papa's participant resolution, followed by R. Yochanan's rejection of Reish Lakish's explanation

argumentFlow.label: R. Yochanan: even a complete return would not have brought the Shechina
argumentFlow.speaker: R. Yochanan
argumentFlow.text: R. Yochanan answered that even had all Babylonian Jews ascended in the days of Ezra, the Shechina would not have rested in the Second Temple. He begins a proof from 'may God enlarge Yefet, and let him dwell in the tents of Shem,' but the daf cuts off on the word 'even' before the proof is completed.

sourceRefs.note: Final point cut off mid-citation, continuing on 10a

visualizableElements.item: Reish Lakish's wall + silver image for a complete return versus door + cedar for a partial return, followed by R. Yochanan's rejection of return size as the reason the Shechina did not rest in the Second Temple.
visualizableElements.label: Wall vs. door: two visions of aliyah

visualizableElements.item: Two alternate pairings for who was in the Jordan, per Rav Papa: (A) Reish Lakish swimming, Ze'iri extending the hand; (B) R. Elazar swimming, Rabbah bar bar Chana extending the hand. Both the swimmer and the hand-extender change between the two options.
visualizableElements.label: The Jordan River pairings

quizSeeds.question: What is sasmagor, and what two things does the Gemara say it represents?
quizSeeds.answer: Literally, per Ulla, a worm that hollows cedar from within. R. Abba adds that it alludes to the bat kol - the diminished form of divine communication that remained after the last prophets died.

quizSeeds.question: What are Rav Papa's two possible pairings for who was in the Jordan, and does 9b end by confirming either one?
quizSeeds.answer: Either Reish Lakish was swimming with Ze'iri extending the hand, or R. Elazar was swimming with Rabbah bar bar Chana extending the hand. R. Yochanan's subsequent rejection concerns Reish Lakish's incomplete-return explanation, not which pairing is correct; his proof continues on 10a.

misconceptions.misconception: 9b ends with R. Yochanan confirming that Reish Lakish's rebuke was justified.
misconceptions.correction: 9b ends mid-citation on a different, further point about Ezra's generation and the Shechina - not with any such confirmation. That point continues on 10a.

misconceptions.misconception: Rav Papa's second pairing is 'Rabbah bar bar Chana swimming, R. Elazar extending the hand.'
misconceptions.correction: It is the reverse: R. Elazar was the one swimming, and Rabbah bar bar Chana extended the hand to him - matching Rashi's own gloss on this passage.

rashiTranslations.en: 'That they delayed their bird-offerings' - for the women would bring them at the completion of their days of childbirth, to be purified so as to eat consecrated food, and they were arrogant men and were lax in offering them, and the women

would wait there until they offered them, and so were delayed from returning to their place, to their husbands, and they thereby kept the women from procreation. 'Mehishtarea' - he expounds it as a notarikon,
'from ruling, one companion'. 'Two companions' - the image that Manasseh set up in the Sanctuary. 'Tzarah' is a term of rivalry, like two wives to one man, 'and her rival provoked her' (1 Samuel 1),

'and you shall not take a woman to her sister, to be a rival to her' (Leviticus 18). 'Its heads judge for a bribe' - the end of the verse is 'yet they lean upon the Lord, saying, is not the Lord in our midst' etc.
'And upon them' - it refers to the First Temple. 'And three'
'decrees' - 'a field', 'ruins', and 'high places of a forest'.
And 'iyin' means ruin, from 'with the broom of destruction' (Isaiah 14),
like 'and hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies' (ibid. 28).
'Whose sin was revealed' - they did not conceal
their transgressions. 'Their end was revealed' - 'when seventy years are completed
for Babylon I will remember you'
(Jeremiah 29). 'The latter, whose sin was not revealed'
- the people of the Second Temple were wicked
in secret. 'The Temple will prove it' - the Temple building.
'Set your eyes on the Temple' - the building of the Temple is a witness for you
in a matter that did not return to us but did return to the former ones.
'I hate you' - all the people of Babylon who did not go up
in the days of Ezra, and who thereby prevented the Divine Presence from coming
to rest again in the Second Temple. 'You would have been likened'
'to silver' - which does not rot; so too you would not have been
lacking the Divine Presence. 'Like doors' - a gate that has
two doors in it: one opens and its fellow
closes; so too you went up only in halves. 'That the rot'
'controls it' - part of it a worm eats
from within, and part of it remains; so too part of the vision of
the Divine Presence was there, but not all of it. 'What is'
'cedar' - what is this 'you were likened to a cedar' that he said? 'Ulla said:'
'sasmagor' - it crushes it and scrapes it
from within; sasmagor is the name of a worm. 'What is'
'sasmagor' - that is to say, why were they in the Second
Temple likened to sasmagor with regard to the resting of the Divine Presence?
'Rabbi Abba said: a bat kol' - there remained for them
just as there remains of the cedar a small part.
'Cast a man between them' - either the one bathing
changes, or the one who extended the hand: if it was Rabbi Shimon ben
Lakish who was bathing, Ze'iri extended him the hand;
or Rabba bar bar Chana extended him the hand
and Rabbi Elazar was the one bathing. 'When he came' - Rabbi Shimon
ben Lakish came before Rabbi Yochanan and recounted
to him: thus did I say to so-and-so.
'Even though' - the comment is completed on 10a.

glossary.en: Baseless hatred - hatred without cause. Identified by the Talmud as the sin that caused the destruction of the Second Temple and the longer exile.
Degradation of sacred offerings - a sin of Eli's sons who seized raw meat before the fat was burned on the altar, treating sacred service as an opportunity for personal benefit.
Heavenly voice - the diminished form of divine communication that replaced direct prophecy after the last prophets (Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi) died.
A cedar-destroying rot. The passage connects it to the bat kol that remained after prophecy departed, within Reish Lakish's wall-and-door interpretation of the incomplete return with Ezra.
